prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Long headers, short data (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Region" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 50px
  col 2: header "Quarterly revenue (USD, millions)" · longest unbreakable word 68px · one-line width 240px
  col 3: header "Year-over-year growth rate" · longest unbreakable word 51px · one-line width 194px
  col 4: header "Number of active enterprise customers" · longest unbreakable word 76px · one-line width 281px
  col 5: header "Net promoter score" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 140px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare regional revenue, growth, enterprise customer counts, and customer sentiment.","reading":"Readers scan across each region to relate its measures, and down each metric to compare regions. The long headers can occupy several lines while the short data rows remain compact.","groups":["Region identifies each row; its labels anchor comparisons across all four measures.","Revenue and year-over-year growth describe financial performance.","Enterprise customer count and net promoter score describe the customer base and its sentiment."] ,"keep_intact":["Region names and abbreviations","Numeric values, percentages, and other individual data values","Individual words and the USD currency identifier"],"may_wrap":["Long headers at natural word boundaries, including the revenue unit in parentheses","The shorter Region header should remain on one line"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[75,158,145,205,136],"idea":"Give the longest customer-count header the most space while retaining a balanced rhythm among the other measures."},{"name":"B","widths":[80,180,150,180,129],"idea":"Give revenue and customer count equal prominence as absolute measures, with narrower columns for growth and sentiment."},{"name":"C","widths":[80,140,140,260,99],"idea":"Prioritize the exceptionally long enterprise-customer header and accept deeper wrapping in the other metric headers."}]}
